Question:
Suppose that one of every \(500\) people in a certain population has a particular disease, which displays no symptoms. A blood test is available for screening for this disease. For a person who has this disease, the test always turns out positive.

For a person who does not have the disease, however, there is a \(2\%\) false positive rate. In other words, for such people, \(98\%\) of the time the test will turn out negative, but \(2\%\) of the time the test will turn out positive and will incorrectly indicate that the person has the disease.

Let \(p\) be the probability that a person who is chosen at random from this population and gets a positive test result actually has the disease. Which of the following is closest to \(p?\)
Solution:
A positive result can come from either a person with the disease or a false positive. We must compare the first group with all positive results.

Represent the given rates by proportional counts for \(25{,}000\) tested people. Scaling all the counts equally does not change the fraction we want. The disease group has
\[
\frac{25{,}000}{500}=50
\]
people, and all of their tests are positive. The disease-free group has \(24{,}950\) people and contributes
\[
2\%\cdot24{,}950=499
\]
false positives. Therefore, among the \(50+499=549\) positive-result units, \(50\) correspond to people with the disease. Hence
\[
p=\frac{50}{549}.
\]
The choices are ordered as
\[
\frac1{98}<\frac1{11}<p<\frac19<\frac{49}{99}<\frac{98}{99},
\]
so only \(\frac1{11}\) and \(\frac19\) can be closest. Their distances from \(p\) are
\[
p-\frac1{11}=\frac1{6039},
\qquad
\frac19-p=\frac{121}{6039}.
\]
Thus the closest choice is \(\boxed{\frac1{11}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
